title: Sleeping Less Than Six Hours a Night Raises Your Osteoarthritis Risk by Up to 40 Per Cent. Night-Shift Workers Face Even Worse Odds.
excerpt: A half-million-person WashU study links short sleep and disrupted circadian rhythms to accelerated joint damage, with implications for every South Asian working late shifts abroad.
body:
A study of nearly 500,000 people has found that consistently sleeping fewer than six hours a night raises the risk of developing osteoarthritis in the hip or knee by 20 to 40 per cent compared with sleeping around seven hours. For people who regularly work night shifts, the numbers are even more alarming: a 24 per cent higher risk of knee osteoarthritis and a 28 per cent greater likelihood of eventually needing a total knee replacement.

The research, led by Dr Elizabeth Yanik at Washington University School of Medicine and published in *Arthritis Care & Research*, drew on the UK Biobank, one of the world's largest longitudinal health databases. What makes the findings especially notable is that the elevated risks held even after researchers controlled for body weight, physical activity, and other known risk factors for joint disease. In other words, poor sleep appears to be an independent driver of joint deterioration, not merely a side effect of pain or obesity.

## Why Sleep Matters for Your Cartilage

The mechanism is straightforward in principle but devastating in practice. During deep sleep, the body runs its most intensive repair cycle. Anti-inflammatory cytokines rise, growth hormone surges, and damaged cartilage receives a small but critical window of restoration. Cut that window short, night after night, and the body enters a state of chronic low-grade inflammation. Cartilage, which has almost no blood supply of its own, is especially vulnerable. It cannot compensate for missed repair time by catching up later.

The study also found that the knee suffered more than the hip. Researchers believe this may reflect differences in how circadian-regulated biology interacts with the mechanical loads each joint bears. The knee absorbs far more impact during daily movement, and if nightly repair processes are disrupted, it accumulates damage faster.

## The Night-Shift Problem Is a Diaspora Problem

For the South Asian diaspora in the United States, United Kingdom, and Canada, these findings land with particular force. A disproportionate number of Indian-origin professionals work in healthcare, IT, and logistics, sectors where night shifts and rotating schedules are routine. Nurses pulling 12-hour overnight rotations, software engineers on graveyard standby for US-India time zones, warehouse workers covering late shifts at fulfilment centres: the study's night-shift cohort maps directly onto a significant segment of the diaspora workforce.

India itself has one of the highest rates of knee osteoarthritis in the world, driven by genetic predisposition, diet, and occupational patterns. The combination of that baseline risk with disrupted sleep in Western work environments creates a compounding effect that few NRIs are aware of.

## What the Numbers Mean in Practice

The 20 to 40 per cent increased risk translates to real consequences at scale. Osteoarthritis is already the most common form of arthritis globally, affecting over 500 million people. Knee replacement surgery, which the study found to be significantly more likely among night-shift workers, carries a recovery period of three to six months, costs between $30,000 and $50,000 in the US without insurance complications, and is not always fully covered for younger patients.

One particularly important finding was that the associations appeared even among participants who had no chronic joint pain at the start of the study. This suggests that poor sleep is contributing to the development of osteoarthritis rather than simply being a symptom of existing joint problems.

## What You Can Actually Do

The study's lead researchers emphasised that the findings are not fatalistic. Sleep is modifiable. For those who cannot avoid night-shift work, the evidence points to several strategies: maintaining a consistent sleep schedule even on days off, using blackout curtains and blue-light blocking during daytime sleep, and prioritising seven hours of total sleep regardless of when the window falls.

For the broader population, the message is simpler: treat sleep as joint protection. The same way you would not skip stretching before a long run, you should not treat six hours of broken sleep as normal. Your cartilage is keeping score, even if your knees have not started complaining yet.

**Sources:** Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis; *Arthritis Care & Research* (2026); UK Biobank dataset
